title: Judge Says California Must Keep Counting Ballots as They Are
summary:
A federal judge in Los Angeles has rejected a request that would have changed how California handles some ballots in the middle of voting. On Wednesday, U.S. District Judge David O. Carter turned down a Trump administration request to stop the state from processing the ballots of up to 20,000 people it alleged were likely noncitizens.

The ruling came as more than 3.7 million people had already voted in California. The state mails ballots to all 23 million registered voters, and court filings show more than 500,000 ballots had already been processed, with envelopes verified and ballots removed. Once that happens, county officials testified, a ballot can no longer be matched to its voter.

Carter wrote that separating the ballots now would wreak havoc and disrupt an election already underway. He said it would risk disenfranchising an untold number of voters, chill election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens. He argued it would work like purging voters, violating the National Voting Rights Act rule against changing voter rolls within 90 days of an election.

The administration sued California election officials in mid-October, saying they missed a 48-hour deadline to review a list of 20,000 people it alleged were likely noncitizens. It asked the judge to require the state to wait to count those ballots until each voter's immigration status could be verified.

Justice Department lawyers said they would immediately appeal. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli argued that segregating a ballot does not stop it from being counted later, saying it was designed to preserve the status quo and prevent the vote from being diluted by illegal ballots. Carter rejected the claim that California was blocking federal enforcement, noting prosecutors had already arrested 28 noncitizens who had allegedly voted or registered to vote illegally.
why_it_matters: Rules about counting ballots in the middle of voting affect whether eligible votes are counted, so court decisions during an election can shape trust in the result.

Taking away or blocking a person's right to vote.

Removing names from a list, here removing voters from the voter rolls.
Made weaker in effect, here used to mean votes counting for less because of illegal votes.
The way things are now, kept unchanged.

background_read: In the United States, states run elections, including mailing ballots to registered voters and checking envelopes before ballots are counted.
Once a ballot is removed from its envelope, it is kept secret and cannot be traced back to the person who cast it.
Federal law limits changes to voter lists close to an election, to avoid removing eligible voters by mistake.
A court can be asked to change how ballots are handled, and a ruling can be appealed to a higher court.

└─ WHERE: California, in a federal court in Los Angeles.
